34.text:
The command, the obedience and the refusal are in one sentence here, and the weight of the verse falls on the clause that separates them. "And remember when We said to the angels" is again a reminder rather than a first telling, and the address includes them as a body. "Prostrate before Adam" states the act and its direction in three words, and the sources dwell on that direction, since the prostration is to Adam and not of worship to him, a distinction the legal discussions need. "so they all did" is given without exception among the angels and without any description of reluctance, and the commentators notice that the text keeps the angels alone here, though other beings stand in the same account. "but not Iblîs" is the hinge, and the verse does not name a reason yet. "who refused and acted arrogantly, becoming unfaithful" then gives the three steps in one clause, the refusal, the arrogance, and the unfaithfulness it ends in. The order is stopped at, since the refusal comes first and the pride after it, and the sources take the last word of the clause as the outcome rather than the motive, so the verse does not have to say what he believed. What he was asked to do is treated as an honour laid on Adam and a test of the hearers at the same time, and the excuses given in the verses that follow, a difference of material and a claim of precedence, are what the legal and spiritual discussions work with here, one of them ruling on the direction of a prostration and the other on what pride does to a person who knows the command.

**The command to prostrate.**

And mention when We said to the angels ‘Prostrate yourselves to Adam’ a prostration that is a bow of salutation; so they prostrated themselves except Iblīs the father of the jinn who was among the angels he refused to prostrate and disdained became proud and said I am better than he Q. 712; and so he became one of the disbelievers according to God’s knowledge. (And when We said unto the angels: Prostrate yourselves before Adam), a prostration of salutation, (they fell prostrate, all save Iblis. He demurred through pride) to follow his Lord's command. Allah reveals that He told the angels to prostrate to Adam out of recognition and respect, so they prostrated to him, eager to do as He told them, except for Iblīs, or Satan, who was originally from the jinn.

**To Adam, and in what sense.**

With regard to the question of prostration, we may add that, according to some authentic scholars, Salah, the basic form of Islamic worship, comprises of four kinds of actions - standing upright, bowing, sitting down, and prostrating oneself; the first two of these, standing up and sitting down, are actions which one habitually does in the course of one's daily chores, and which one also performs as acts of worship in the course of a Salah (prayer), but the other two, bowing down and prostrating oneself, are actions which one does not go through as a matter of habit, and which are characteristically associated with Salah (prayer) and Ibadah (worship); hence it is that the Islamic Shari'ah has identified them with acts of worship, and forbidden the Muslims to bow down or prostrate themselves before anyone other than Allah. But the Holy Qur'an mentions the angels alone, because when superior beings like the angels were required to show their respect for Adam inferior creatures like the jinns must, it goes without saying, have been ordered to do the same.

**Was Iblîs one of the angels.**

Although Iblis was not an angel, he was trying - and pretending - to imitate the angels' behavior and deeds, and this is why he was also included in the command to the angels to prostrate before Adam. It is also said that it was in Allah's foreknowledge that Satan was to become a disbeliever; as it is said that he was the first unbeliever ever. Due to the excellence of his worship, Allah had entered Iblīs into the company of the angels; but he then returned to his lowly nature, refusing to prostrate as Allah told him to, and becoming proud towards Adam, leading to him becoming a disbeliever. The command came to the angels, "All of you go to Adam's throne and prostrate yourself before Adam.

**Refused, acted arrogantly, became unfaithful.**

(And so became a disbeliever) after this because he refused to comply with Allah's command. He said, 'I was created from fire, and he was created from clay.' Therefore, the first error ever committed was arrogance, for the enemy of Allah was too arrogant to prostrate before Adam. The word literally means one who was far from the truth, and from the mercy of God.

**Two rulings that hang off this verse.**

For example, making pictures of living things has been totally banned; prostrating oneself before somebody, even as a mark of respect, has been forbidden; it is not permissible to offer one's Salah (prayer) at those hours of the day which the infidels had reserved for worshipping their gods, for even this slight and external correspondence might lead to 'association'; and, according to a Hadith reported by Muslim, one is not allowed to call one's slave an " abd" nor is a slave allowed to call his master a "rabb " - the words respectively signify "a slave" and 'one who gives nurture', and are as such harmless, but they can be misconstrued, and may mislead ignorant slaves or helpless and subjugated people into the worship of their masters: hence the prohibition. The word literally means one who was far from the truth, and from the mercy of God.

**What else the same passage holds.**

The episode recounted in the foregoing verses has shown how the angels came to learn that Adam was superior to them in so far as he possessed the forms of knowledge necessary for the function of divine vice regency, while they themselves did not, nor did the jinns. Now, Allah willed to manifest this superiority in a visible and concrete form. So, He commanded the angels to prostrate themselves before Adam in his honour. They obeyed except Iblis or Satan who, in his pride, refused to do so. If we go by the words of the Holy Qur'an, the command was given to the angels alone, but, in excepting Iblis from those who obeyed, the text also suggests that the command was given to all the created beings that existed at that time and possessed understanding, including the jinns as well as the angels. In this verse, the angels have been commanded to prostrate themselves before Adam . Another verse of the Holy Qur'an tells us that the parents and the brothers of Yusuf (Joseph) on reaching Egypt, prostrated themselves before him (12:100). Evidently such a prostration cannot have been intended as an act of worship, for worshipping anyone other than Allah is an act of association (Shirk) and infidelity (Kufr), and hence cannot possibly be allowed by any Shari ah. So, it appears that in the days of the ancient prophets prostrating oneself before somebody must have been just an act of courtesy or a way of showing one's respect, and enjoyed the same value as we do in our own days things like a simple greeting, a handshake, the kissing of hand, or standing up in someone's honour.

35.text:
Everything in this verse is permission except one clause, and the order matters because the exception is what the next verses turn on. "We cautioned, O Adam! Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please" opens with warning rather than with the gift, and the two halves are quoted together here because the permission is the shape the warning sits inside, and the sources note the word for caution here, since what follows sounds like a favour. "Live with your wife in Paradise and eat as freely as you please" gives the dwelling as shared, the wife named in the same breath, and the eating without reckoning; the commentators take "as freely as you please" to cover whatever they wanted, in any part of the Garden, and the permission to eat is treated as the general rule from which the prohibition is an exception. "but do not approach this tree" is then not a second command but the edge of the first, and the wording, approach rather than eat, is stopped at more than once. "or else you will be wrongdoers" ends without naming a punishment at all, which is how the discussion of what the prohibition actually lays on them begins, since the consequence is stated as a condition of the act and not as a sentence. The dwelling with his wife is taken by the sources as the first of the permissions in this passage and the pair are named together on purpose, and the verse after this records the slip.

**Dwell, and eat freely.**

And We said ‘Adam dwell anta ‘you’ of ‘dwell you’ here reiterates the concealed pronoun of the person of the verb uskun so that it wa-zawjuk may be made a supplement to it; and your wife Eve Hawwā’ — who was created from his left rib — in the Garden and eat thereof of its food easefully of anything without restrictions where you desire; but do not come near this tree to eat from it and this was wheat or a vine or something else lest you be become evildoers’ that is transgressors. Allah told Adam to live with his wife, Eve, in the Garden, with nothing to ruin their bliss.

**The scope of the permission.**

In allowing Adam and Hawwa to eat at pleasure, and in forbidding them to go near the tree, Allah used, according to the text of the Holy Qur'an, the verbs for the dual number, thus including both in the address. But the words of the Holy Qur'an do not exclude the other interpretation that both the events took place in Paradise, but that he had not been told at that time where he was to live, which was done later.

**What the words do not exclude.**

When Adam and Hawwa were sent to live in Paradise, they were allowed to eat whatever they liked 'at pleasure' - the Arabic word in the text being 'Raghadan' ‌ which signifies provision for which one does not have to work, and which is never exhausted nor falls short. (And We said: O Adam! Dwell thou and thy wife in the Garden) enter you and Eve into Paradise (and eat ye freely (of the fruits) without restriction (thereof where ye will) and whenever you will; (but come not near this tree) but do not eat from this tree, the tree of knowledge, which includes all types and kinds (lest ye become of the wrong-doers), lest you harm yourselves.

**Approach, not eat.**

They were instructed to consume the delightful food from anywhere in the Garden, but also to avoid going near a particular tree which they were forbidden to eat from. If they ate from the prohibited tree, they would become wrongdoers for disobeying Him.

**The end of the warning, and the test that follows.**

(Then the Shaytan made them slip therefrom) either refers to Paradise, and in this case, it means that Shaytan led Adam and Hawwa' away from it, as 'Asim bin Abi An-Najud recited it. Then Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the story of Adam and Eve, saying: Either they would follow the example of the angels and bow to God’s commandments, even if it meant bowing before someone they held inferior to themselves; or else they would be proud like Satan, and refuse to bow to others. This is the test that man faces throughout his entire life. When Adam woke up and saw Hawwa' next to him, it was claimed, he said, 'My flesh and blood, my wife.' Hence, Adam reclined with Hawwa'.

**What else the same passage holds.**

This is a continuation of the story of Adam . When his superiority over the angels and his fitness for the role of vice regent had been announced to the angels and been acknowledged by them, and Iblis had been condemned as an infidel and expelled from Paradise on account of his pride and his defiance of divine authority, Adam and Hawwa , his wife, received a command from Allah to live in Paradise and enjoy its blessings. But they were also instructed not to eat the fruit of a particular tree. Now, having been disgraced because of Adam Iblis or Satan had an account to settle with him, and as soon as he got the opportunity, he tricked them into eating from this tree. Because of this error on their part, they too were ordered to leave Paradise, and to go down and live on the earth. They were at the same time warned that their existence on the earth would no longer be full of perpetual bliss as it had been in Paradise, but that there would be dissension and enmity among men, their progeny, which would spoil the joy of earthly life. Since these events took place after Adam had been created and the angels had been commanded to prostrate themselves before him, some scholars have concluded from it that the creation of Adam and the prostration of the angels took place somewhere outside Paradise, and that he was sent there later on. Thus, their life was totally free from all care. They were commanded not to go near a certain tree - which was an emphatic way of asking them not to eat its fruit. The tree has not been given a specific name either in the Holy Qur'an or in the Hadith. Some commentators say that it was wheat, others say that it was a fig-tree or a grape-vine. But it is not really necessary to make specific what the Holy Qur'an has left vague. As to the apple being the fruit concerned, it is only a popular misunderstanding arising from the fact that the Latin word "Malum" means an "apple" as well as a "sin, or evil. According to the Holy Qur'an, it was Satan who 'caused them to slip' (azallahuma). It clearly shows that the error and disobedience of Adam and Hawwa was not of the kind which technically constitutes a sin, but arose out of a misunderstanding produced by Satan. They ate the forbidden fruit, because Satan had cleverly deceived them.16 We may note that in the previous episode the Holy Qur'an used the name Iblis a word which comes from the root Balas 'to be disappointed', and hence signifies "one who has lost all hope of receiving the grace of Allah.

36.text:
“But Satan deceived them” names an action, and “leading to their fall from the ˹blissful˺ state they were in” gives its immediate result. The two parts belong together, but the line does not make Satan the authority who sends them away. “and We said” changes the speaker and the kind of action being described. “Descend from the heavens ˹to the earth˺ as enemies to each other” is a command with a destination and a changed relation among those addressed. The next words, “You will find in the earth a residence and provision for your appointed stay,” do not reverse that command. They describe what life there will include. A residence is a place to live, and provision is what sustains life there, but “for your appointed stay” sets a limit on both. The verse therefore moves through four points: deception, loss of the state they had enjoyed, descent under a command, and an earthly life that has its own provision and end. It follows the earlier permission to Adam and his wife, which had one limit, and leads into Adam’s words of repentance in the next verse. The story does not stop with the fall, but neither does it call the new residence a return to the Garden. The contrast between residence and provision also matters: one is a place, the other what sustains life there, not a promise that the first comfort is restored. The phrase “as enemies to each other” changes the sentence from a description of Satan's action to a description of the relations that will shape life on earth. The ending gives ordinary life its own terms. They will live and be provided for, but only for a span. The verse names no details of that span, so it closes with a limit rather than a new timetable.

**The first verb and the tree.**

The opening verb has more than one reported reading. One keeps the sense of Satan making Adam and his wife slip. Another takes it as his causing them to leave the Garden. The difference is not only a choice of English verb. The form fa-azallahuma presents them as made to slip, while fa-azalahuma is read as causing them to be removed from their place. Both readings retain Satan's role, but the second puts the emphasis on their departure rather than the manner of their eating. The commentators also differ on what “therefrom” refers to, the Garden or the forbidden tree. Al-Hasan and Qatadah take the wording with the tree in view, as Satan tripping them because of it. These readings should not be collapsed into an identification of the tree. Reported guesses include a grapevine, barley, a date palm and a fig tree, but Abu Jaʿfar ibn Jarīr concludes that neither the Qur'an nor the authentic Sunnah identifies it, and that knowing which tree it was brings no benefit. The text leaves that detail open. Whatever sense is preferred for the verb, the next clause makes the deception the immediate cause of their departure, while the descent itself is announced as God's command.

**Satan's role and the command.**

The adjacent clauses keep two kinds of agency distinct. One explanation says that the Qur'an can attribute the bringing out to Satan because he served as a means, while the actual sending down followed God's command. That reading does not erase Satan's deception or give him independent power. It distinguishes the means from the authority that carries out the descent. The sources also ask how Satan reached Adam and Hawwaʾ after he had been expelled for refusing to prostrate. They offer possibilities, not a single established route. He may have planted a suggestion from afar, appeared in another form, entered secretly, or misled them as he left the Garden or after they were on earth. The verse does not decide among these explanations. It does say that Satan assured them on oath that he was a well-wisher, a detail linked to 7:21. That false assurance explains how the temptation was presented, but it does not answer how Satan gained access. The oath also shows that the deception worked by exploiting trust. Its force comes from promising good while urging a step that the Lord had already forbidden. The act remains a choice made under false counsel, and the false counsel does not turn the forbidden act into permission. This is a different question from the route Satan took into the Garden. The verse names what he did, while the commentaries offer possible settings for how he did it. Keeping those questions separate prevents a later narrative from being mistaken for what this verse itself states.

**The parties to the enmity.**

The command to descend is followed by the words “as enemies to each other,” but the verse does not name every person included in that address. The explanations differ. One includes Satan with Adam, Hawwaʾ and their descendants if Satan had not yet left the heavens. Another takes him to have been expelled already, so that the words refer to Adam, Hawwaʾ and their descendants, with enmity arising among their children. Other glosses include the serpent and the peacock as well. A concise reading identifies Satan among those sent down, while another focuses on human descendants and the conflicts that will occur among them. These are alternative accounts, not a single list that can safely be combined. Another reading explains the enmity as people wronging one another. The uncertainty concerns the full set of addressees, not the warning that earthly life will include hostility. The following verses turn from that condition to repentance, guidance and the choices made in response.

**A dwelling and provision for a time.**

The last clause describes the life that follows the descent. One gloss describes the dwelling as a place of settlement and the provision as livelihood, lasting until death. Another describes a dwelling, sustenance and a limited life that continues until the Resurrection. A further explanation treats the earth as a temporary dwelling from which its inhabitants will also have to depart. The verse therefore does not say that the earth is empty of good. It names a residence and provision, while also making their duration finite. The account of Adam is thus not only about being removed from the Garden. It opens a history in which people live, receive provision and face enmity, but do so for a measured period. The statement gives earthly provision a limit and directs attention beyond the present life. That limit does not make earthly provisions unreal or meaningless. It says that life on earth is a stage of the story rather than its final home. A practical reading draws a lesson from the preceding command to bow: people can follow what is right even when pride resists it, or follow Satan's example and refuse another person's right. That lesson is not another description of the descent. It carries the story forward to the conduct expected of Adam's descendants.

**An allusive reading of the departure.**

A spiritual reading treats Adam's departure not as proof of low worth, but as a movement toward a greater beauty and a more demanding love. In that reading, the ease of the Garden is set beside an aspiration that reaches beyond ease. This is an allusion about the soul's longing, not a report about the route Satan took or a replacement for the verse's account of the descent. It offers a different kind of reflection on why loss and return can stand together in the same passage. The next verse supplies the narrative's next step: Adam receives words from his Lord, and repentance is accepted.

37.text:
“Then Adam was inspired with words ˹of prayer˺ by his Lord” puts the receiving of words before the result. “so He accepted his repentance” moves from what Adam received to what God does with it. “Surely He is the Accepter of Repentance, Most Merciful” closes with the character of that response, rather than with details of Adam's words. The opening “Then” connects this verse to the deception and descent just described. It does not present the mistake as the end of the story. The order is important: words are given, repentance is accepted, and mercy is named. The verse itself does not quote the words, and the next verse broadens the passage from Adam's return to guidance for all who will follow it. A reader can see the main point before the commentaries identify different prayers and reports: Adam turns back and the Lord receives that repentance. The closing description is not Adam's own verdict. The verse grounds acceptance in God's merciful character. The explanations that follow identify possible wording, while this opening account already states what happens after Adam turns back.

**What the words refer to.**

The verse leaves Adam's words unnamed, and the commentaries preserve more than one account of them. A grammatical reading makes the words the subject, so they come to Adam rather than being words he takes from his Lord. Another explanation describes him as learning these words from God and says they became a way to repentance for him and his descendants. These readings keep the source of the words with God and make their purpose clear, but they do not by themselves identify their wording. A widely cited identification is the prayer in 7:23: “Our Lord! We have wronged ourselves. If You forgive us not, and bestow not upon us Your mercy, we shall certainly be of the losers.” Mujahid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan and Qatadah are among those who connect this prayer to Adam's words. A concise gloss gives the same prayer and makes the connection explicit. The passage in al-Aʿrāf supplies a complete confession, while this verse here emphasizes that the words came from Adam's Lord and that his repentance was accepted.

**Another report about Adam's words.**

A second report gives the words as a longer exchange. As-Suddi reports that Ibn ʿAbbās explained the verse with a longer exchange. Adam recalls that God created him and gave him life, then recalls being shown mercy after he sneezed. He asks whether God's mercy comes before anger and whether repentance can return him to Paradise. The point of this account is the return Adam seeks, not an identity for the forbidden tree. Al-Hakim recorded the report through Ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās. He described its chain as ṣaḥīḥ and noted that al-Bukhārī and Muslim did not include it in their collections. That statement belongs to the report as the source gives it. It is not a grading added here, and no number is supplied. The two explanations should remain distinct: one identifies the words with the prayer in 7:23, while another preserves a reported dialogue about mercy and return.

**Repentance after a real loss.**

The acceptance of Adam's repentance does not make the earlier disobedience insignificant. The practical lesson describes the forbidden tree as a test of whether a person will remain within God's limits. Eating from it meant the loss of Paradise and of God's grace, yet that loss was not beyond repair. A person could turn back, correct his actions and ask forgiveness. The verse's order matters here. Adam first receives words, then God accepts his repentance, and then the verse names God as the One who repeatedly accepts repentance and shows mercy. The account is neither that wrongdoing has no consequence nor that a person is trapped forever by one failure. A concise explanation describes Adam as turning to God and being forgiven. The passage that follows widens this possibility: guidance will come to people on earth, and the next verse will describe the promise to those who follow it.

**The names at the end.**

“Accepter of Repentance” names more than a single pardon. The sources explain it as overlooking misdeeds and accepting the one who returns, while “Most Merciful” describes the care with which that return is met. Other verses connect these names to the same pattern of repentance: God forgives the one who regrets an error and returns to Him. This keeps the last clause attached to the narrative rather than turning it into a general slogan. Adam's repentance is the example in view, but the names of God describe why repentance remains possible for others too.

**An allusion to what is left unspoken.**

An allusive reading notices that the verse does not disclose the words Adam received. It treats that silence as a protected compact between God and Adam, and imagines the answer as a heart that does not turn its love elsewhere. This is a spiritual reflection on the verse's restraint, not a competing historical report of what Adam said. The two registers can sit beside one another so long as the allusion is not mistaken for the wording of the prayer. The account itself ends where it began, with words given by God and mercy shown to Adam.

38.text:
“We said, Descend all of you!” brings the command forward again, but the verse does not end at the descent. “Then when guidance comes to you from Me” places another event ahead, and “whoever follows it” makes the response open to each person addressed. “there will be no fear for them” and “nor will they grieve” give the promised result in two parts. The verse moves from a plural departure to guidance that will come later, then to an individual condition, and finally to the outcome for those who follow. It also continues the movement from Adam's accepted repentance: the way back in the previous verse becomes an offer to more than Adam alone. Life on earth is not presented as guidance-free. The previous verse named a residence and provision, while this one adds a path through that life. “from Me” locates the source of the guidance, and “whoever follows it” keeps the promise tied to a response. The next verse sets the opposite response beside this promise, so the warning and the invitation are meant to be read together.

**Who is included in the command.**

The phrase “Descend all of you” repeats the movement from the preceding verse, but the explanations do not give one identical list of those addressed. Some explanations describe Adam, Hawwaʾ and their descendants as going to earth, and one also names Satan among those sent down before guidance is promised to their offspring. Other readings extend the address to the descendants. A wider list includes Adam, Eve, the serpent, the peacock and Satan, then turns to Adam's progeny when it explains the guidance that will come. These details belong to the commentators' explanations of the plural, not to names supplied in this verse. The verse itself moves from “all of you” to “you” without pausing to identify each addressee. The point common to the readings is that the command opens life on earth, and the guidance that follows is not limited to Adam alone.

**What guidance brings.**

The sources understand guidance as something that will arrive after the descent, not as a private memory of what Adam already knew. One explanation describes it as a Book and a prophet. Another says that books and messengers will be sent to Adam's offspring, and quotes Abu al-ʿAliyah's explanation that guidance includes prophets, messengers, clear signs and plain explanation. A concise gloss likewise connects it with the prophets and belief in them. The wording “from Me” matters because the direction comes from God, while “whoever follows it” leaves the response with each person. The promise is not restricted to one generation or one individual. It follows the universal command to descend with a way to recognize and follow what is sent. The practical lesson links the offer to Adam's earlier mistake: loss is not irretrievable when a person turns back and seeks forgiveness. The guidance is the continuing direction by which later people can respond faithfully.

**Fear and grief are not the same.**

The promise has two parts, and one explanation distinguishes them. Fear concerns an expected trouble or pain ahead. Grief is sorrow over losing something valued or failing to attain what was sought. Together the two phrases describe comfort across what is still to come and what has already been lost. The commentary also notes a difference in the Arabic construction: “no fear for them” is expressed as a noun, while “they will not grieve” is a verb with the people themselves as its subject. That explanation takes the difference to mean that freedom from fear is stated generally, while complete freedom from worldly grief belongs to those who have fully submitted their desires to God's will. It still reserves awe of God and concern for the next life. This is one interpretation, not a claim that a believer never feels an ordinary reaction to danger. The same explanation points to Moses feeling fear when his staff became a serpent. It describes that as an instinctive physical reaction, then offers another explanation in which Moses feared the event might mislead the Israelites. A further gloss ties the phrases to future torment and sorrow over what was left behind. It also records a reading that the promise lasts through the Hereafter, with no fear when death is slain and no grief when the Fire is closed. The promise in this verse concerns the final security of those who follow guidance, and should not be used to deny the natural emotions the sources themselves acknowledge.

**The promise after descent.**

The descent and the promise are not competing endings. One explanation says that Adam's arrival on earth continues after his pardon, but the passage now speaks of the wisdom and responsibility of life there. An allusive reading sees the return to earth and the promise of guidance side by side: the one sent away is also given glad tidings of a return if the heart is inclined toward it. A practical reading makes a related point. Adam's loss was real, but turning in repentance remained possible. This verse then makes guidance the condition for the promised safety, and verse 39 gives the other side of the choice. The passage holds both together, a life on earth with its difficulty and the promise of a way through it.

39.text:
“But those who disbelieve and deny Our signs will be the residents of the Fire” sets the other response beside the promise in the previous verse. “They will be there forever” makes the duration part of the warning, not a temporary pause. The first phrase describes those people by two connected acts, disbelief and denial of signs. The second tells where that response leads. Because the verse begins with “But,” its meaning depends on what came just before: guidance has been offered, and a promise has been made to those who follow it. The verse does not add a new episode or a different command. It states the other outcome in direct terms. The Fire is called a residence too, but unlike the earth's residence in verse 36, this stay is not limited to an appointed time. That contrast gives weight to the final words. The next verse moves from this general warning to the address of the Children of Israel, whose response to God's favors and covenant becomes the subject.

**The contrast with those who follow guidance.**

Verse 38 promises safety to those who follow guidance. This verse begins with “But” and describes the other response as both disbelief and denial. The contrast is not simply between two destinations. One group accepts what comes from God and follows it, while the other rejects the signs. The commentaries place the two verses together and link the warning to the earlier promise. A practical reading takes the refusal to acknowledge truth as a return to Satan's path and as a failure of the test that has run through the account of Adam. That application should be kept close to the text. It concerns refusal of the signs and truth, not every disagreement between people or every mistaken reading. The warning addresses a settled response to what is shown, and verse 40 will turn from that general contrast to a named people and the covenant placed before them.

**What the denial includes.**

One gloss explains “Our signs” as Scripture and the Messenger, so the denial is not confined to looking at a sign and failing to recognize it. It includes rejecting the guidance brought to people. The short glosses describe the residents of the Fire as the people who deny the signs and books. A commentary connects the statement to Qur'an 20:124, where turning away from God's Reminder is linked to a life of hardship and being raised blind on the Day of Resurrection. It calls that passage similar to the warning here. The cross-reference helps show that the subject is deliberate turning away, not lack of access to the words. An allusive reading treats denial as receiving favor without gratitude or recognition of truth. That is a spiritual reflection on what denial does to the heart, not a separate cause added to the verse.

**The permanence of the outcome.**

The final sentence leaves no temporary interval in the warning. One gloss explains abiding as enduring without perishing or leaving. Another says the residents do not die or get released, and a further explanation likewise describes the Fire's people as remaining there without a way out. These are explanations of “forever,” not separate punishments to be added to it. The verse is brief because it completes the contrast set up in 38. Its warning is severe, and the words do not soften that severity. At the same time, it belongs to a passage that has just set out guidance and the promise attached to following it. Verse 40 will now address the Children of Israel directly, recalling favors and calling them to keep their covenant.

40.text:
“O children of Israel!” names the people addressed before the commands begin. “Remember My favours upon you” asks them to bring past gifts into view, not as a memory detached from the present but as the reason for a response. “Fulfil your covenant and I will fulfil Mine” places an obligation beside a promise. The first half asks the people to keep what they owe, and the second promises God's response. “and stand in awe of Me ˹alone˺” brings the address to its final focus: the fear and reverence due here are directed to God alone. The sequence is deliberate. A named people are reminded of favor, called to keep a covenant, and told where their deepest fear must be directed. This comes after the account of Adam and the promise of guidance for all who follow it. The address now turns to a particular community and asks whether they will respond to what God has given them. The following verses make the covenant more specific, linking it to belief in what has been sent down. This verse gives the frame before that detail: remember, fulfil, and fear God alone. “Remember My favours” also prevents the covenant from sounding like a bargain invented by the people. The gifts come first. The covenant is a response to them, and the promise makes clear that the response is met by God's own generosity. The last word, “alone,” prevents the appeal from being divided between God and the pressures of other people. The verse is therefore both reminder and demand, not only a recollection of an earlier history. It asks its hearers to act now on what they remember, rather than treat the past as a finished story.

**Israel, Jacob, and the people addressed.**

The name Israel refers to Jacob, who is also called Yaʿqub, so “children of Israel” addresses the descendants of a prophet rather than an unnamed crowd. One explanation says the name recalls their ancestor as a servant of God and calls them to follow his example of worship and obedience. The name gives the audience a family history, but it does not allow them to rely on that history alone. The command is addressed to them in the present. The sūrah's address to the People of the Book continues through a long stretch, but it opens here with a reminder of kinship and favor before it describes their failures. Another strand connects the address with the arrival of a prophet. It treats the sending of a prophet as the greatest favor to a people, because it opens a road to salvation. The title therefore carries both honor and responsibility. They are named through Jacob, but the passage asks them to answer God's current call.

**The favors to remember.**

The sources give examples of what this favor includes. One short gloss recalls the rescue of their forefathers from Pharaoh, the parting of the sea and the clouds sent as shelter. Another adds Scripture and the messenger, escape from Pharaoh and drowning, and the provision of honey and quails. Mujahid identifies water made to gush from stones, manna and quails, and rescue from Pharaoh. Abu al-ʿAliyah emphasizes the prophets and books sent among them. These lists are not identical, but they point to the same range of care: rescue from oppression, food and shelter, and revelation. The address also sits within the larger discussion of the People of the Book, who had earlier revelation and were now being invited to recognize the Qur'an. Remembering the favor is therefore more than counting benefits. It means recognizing the giver and responding with gratitude, belief and obedience. The command recalls the past in order to shape what the audience will do with the message now before them. This range matters because remembrance is not reduced to a single family story or a material list. Escape from Pharaoh addresses political oppression, food and shade meet ordinary need, and revelation gives direction. The next verses return to revelation, so the call to remember is tied to a decision still before the audience.

**What the covenant asks.**

The verse does not spell out every term of the covenant, and the next verses develop it. Qatadah and Mujahid connect the covenant with the agreement described in 5:12. That passage names prayer, alms, belief in God's messengers, support for them and a good loan, followed by forgiveness and entry into gardens. One explanation draws from that list to say that faith in all the messengers, including Muhammad ﷺ, is central. Ibn ʿAbbās is cited for the more focused explanation that the covenant here means believing in and obeying Muhammad. Other explanations preserve more than one formulation. One ties the covenant to the earlier promise of a prophet from the descendants of Ismail. Another describes it more generally as embracing Islam and adhering to it. These readings need not be made into competing contracts. The particular call to recognize Muhammad sits within the broader demand to believe in God's messengers and obey what God has revealed. What the verse requires is not ancestry alone, but loyalty to the revelation that confirms the earlier message. The broader description also guards against reducing the covenant to a single formula or to an inherited promise. Its shared core in these explanations is faith joined to obedience. The list in 5:12 shows that obedience includes worship, generosity and standing with God's messengers, not merely affirming a name.

**The promised return and the fear of God.**

“I will fulfil Mine” is explained as a promise of forgiveness and Paradise for those who keep their side. One gloss also mentions a good life on earth and a beautiful reward on the Day of Judgment. The parallel covenant in 5:12 names forgiveness and admission to gardens. A report transmitted from Ad-Dahhak through Ibn ʿAbbās explains God's fulfilment as being pleased with them and admitting them to Paradise. The covenant's two sides remain distinct. The people are called to fulfill their obligation, and God promises forgiveness and reward. The final command, “stand in awe of Me alone,” joins encouragement to warning. One explanation takes it as fear of God's punishment, with the history of the earlier generations in view. Another connects the command to the pressure Israelite scholars faced: they could fear public opinion, losing their followers and losing income if they spoke openly about the message. This is not a demand to feel no danger. It says fear of people must not overrule the duty owed to God, and so reaches public speech as well as private feeling. The verses that follow make that application explicit by calling them to believe in what has been sent down.

**Keeping an agreement.**

The legal discussion attached to the verse draws a general rule from the command: an agreement must be fulfilled, and breaking a promise is forbidden. The discussion cites a report from Muslim describing the humiliation of promise-breakers on the Day of Judgment, when a flag is placed beside each person in keeping with the seriousness of the breach. No number for this report is supplied in the source, so none is added here. The practical point is already clear from the verse's wording. The covenant is not an abstract idea. It binds the people addressed to truthfulness and obedience, and the promise of reward does not erase the seriousness of breaking it.

**An allusive reading of the covenant.**

An allusive reading takes the two halves of “My covenant” as an image of reciprocal loyalty between God and the servant. It contrasts the call to Israel to remember God's blessings with the call elsewhere to remember God, and reads the covenant as a way of turning gratitude into closeness. This is a spiritual reflection on the verse, not a replacement for the covenant's concrete demands described above. Read alongside those demands, it brings out the movement from favor to gratitude, from gratitude to obedience, and from obedience to the promise of mercy. The verse has begun by naming Israel and ends by narrowing the object of awe to God alone. Its three commands therefore prepare the way for the more detailed appeal that follows.

41.text:
The previous verse calls the Children of Israel to keep their covenant, and this command makes the response concrete. “Believe in My revelations which confirm your Scriptures” begins with acceptance of what God has sent. The words “My revelations” point to a message from God, while “which confirm your Scriptures” connects it with the earlier book already familiar to the audience. This is not a call to treat the two as unrelated. It identifies a continuity that the hearers are asked to recognize. “Do not be the first to deny them or trade them for a fleeting gain” moves from recognition to the danger of refusing the message. The warning about being first is directed to people who know the Scripture and can recognize its confirmation. Their denial could lead others after them to follow the same course. “Trade them for a fleeting gain” gives a second form of refusal, putting a short-lived worldly benefit before the revelations. The gain does not change what the message is or remove responsibility for concealing it. The final phrase, “And be mindful of Me,” turns the audience back to God as the One to fear and obey. It closes the commands with accountability, rather than the benefits that might follow from denial. The order is important: accept the revealed message, do not lead others in rejecting it or exchange it for a temporary advantage, and keep God in view. The last command also changes the measure by which the choice is made. A fleeting gain is temporary, but God remains the One before whom the response to revelation is accountable. The people are not asked merely to recognize a familiar text; they are asked to act on what that recognition means. The short closing words therefore reach back to each earlier part of the sentence.

**The covenant and the confirming message.**

(And fulfill (your obligations to) My covenant (with you) so that I fulfill (My obligations to) your covenant (with Me),) means, 'My covenant that I took from you concerning Prophet Muhammad , when he is sent to you, so that I grant you what I promised you if you believe in him and follow him. And believe in what I have revealed of the Qur’ān confirming that which is with you of the Torah by its agreement with it in respect to affirmation of God’s Oneness and prophethood; and be not the first to disbelieve in it from among the People of the Scripture for those who will come after you will depend on you and so you will bear their sins. The greatest favour that God bestows upon a people is to send His prophet to them, thus opening for them the road to eternal salvation. (And believe in what I have sent down, confirming that which is with you (the Tawrah and the Injil) meaning, the Qur'an that Allah sent down to Muhammad , the unlettered Arab Prophet, as bringer of glad tidings, a warner and a light. (Indeed, Allah took the covenant from the Children of Israel (Jews), and We appointed twelve leaders among them. And Allah said: "I am with you if you perform As-Salah and give Zakah and believe in My Messengers; honor and assist them, and lend a good loan to Allah, verily, I will expiate your sins and admit you to Gardens under which rivers flow (in Paradise)(5:12)."

**Being first to deny.**

The verse, in fact, suggests that the man who is the first to deny and disbelieve will not only incur the sin of his own denial but also bear the additional burden of the sin of misleading all those who follow his example; and will thus have to undergo a multiple punishment. Ibn 'Abbas commented, "Do not become the first to disbelieve in the Qur'an (or Muhammad), while you have more knowledge in it than other people. " Abu Al-'Aliyah commented, "Do not become the first to disbelieve in Muhammad, meaning from among the People of the Book, after you hear that he was sent as a Prophet. (the first to disbelieve therein) means, do not become the first among the Children of Israel to disbelieve in it, for there were people from Quraysh and the Arabs in general who rejected Muhammad before the People of the Book disbelieved in him. Those whose sensitivity to truth was still alive recognized the veracity of his prophethood and followed him. But those for whom religion had become a hereditary tradition found his message unfamiliar and failed to recognize the truth when they heard it; they rejected it and turned against the Prophet. Do not [be the ones to] introduce disbelief kufr as an ongoing practice sunna for surely the responsi bility of the initiator in what he practices is greater than the responsibility of the imitator in what he follows. It follows from here that the man who is in any way responsible for others falling into any kind of sin will have to bear the burden of this sin along with the sinners; similarly, the man who in some way helps others to do a good deed will receive a reward for it along with them. However, soon their religion ceased to be something that they accepted as a matter of conscious decision, and they let it deteriorate into a set of lifeless rituals passed on from one generation to the next.

**An allusive reading of belief.**

The final states of their belief are through eyewitnessing ʿiyān and that is for the elect of the elect.

**The price of refusal.**

And do not sell exchange My signs those that relate to the description of Muhammad in your Book; for a small price for a trivial and temporary affair of this world; that is to say do not suppress this for fear of losing what you hope to earn from lowly individuals among you; and fear Me and none other in this matter. The context makes it clear that it is forbidden to take money from people by misinterpreting or concealing the verses of the Book of Allah in order to please them or to serve their worldly interests. As for the question of taking a wage for teaching the verses of the Holy Qur'an or for reporting them correctly, verse 41 is not concerned with the matter. But it is an important question in itself whether it is permissible to accept wages for teaching the Holy Qur'an. Do not exchange His signs – the verses which He has revealed – for the small price of position or leadership, and avoid His displeasure and punishment. (and buy not with My verses a small price,) means, "Do not substitute faith in My Ayat and belief in My Prophet with the life of this world and its lusts which are minute and bound to end. (and fear Me and Me alone) means, that Allah warns the People of the Book against intentionally hiding the truth and spreading the opposite of it, as well as, against defying the Messenger . In view of the clear prophecies in the Torah of the coming of an Arab Prophet, it would not have been difficult for the Israelites to recognize the truth of his prophethood and believe in him; but to believe in him was not in their worldly interests. It appeared to them that if they accepted the Arab Prophet, their privileged religious position would come to an end and their whole profit structure would be demolished. Over hundreds of years an ecclesiastical structure had developed, in which the Israelites had held pride of place. Being the successors of saints and prophets, they were looked up to for spiritual leadership. Do not prefer your cheap worldly portion ḥaẓẓ over the grandeur of My truth ḥaqq.

42.text:
The call to accept what confirms earlier Scripture is followed by a warning about truth itself. “Do not mix truth with falsehood or hide the truth knowingly” joins two ways of failing to handle what is known. “Do not mix truth with falsehood” warns against placing a false account beside the truth so that the hearer cannot distinguish one from the other. The issue is not an innocent error. The wording moves next to what a person hides, and “knowingly” makes knowledge part of the warning. It concerns a truth that the hearer recognizes and then conceals, whether from fear or from a desire for gain. The first part concerns what is presented; the second concerns what is withheld. Both make a person answerable for the way truth reaches other people. This continues the previous appeal to believe in revelation and not to exchange it for a passing benefit. Belief cannot be separated from honest handling of the message. The warning also leads into the command to establish prayer, give alms and bow with those who bow. The passage thus moves from accepting truth to preserving it clearly, and then to worship and action. The last phrase does not leave room for ignorance as an excuse where knowledge is already present. It describes a deliberate concealment, not simply a lack of understanding. The verse asks the audience to let the truth stand without confusing it with falsehood and without keeping it from those who need to hear it. Its place before the next verse links truthful teaching with visible practice. The first verb pictures a person putting an untrue account alongside a true one, so the listener cannot tell which to accept. The second is different. A person may say nothing false yet keep back a truth that should be made clear. The mention of knowledge points to deliberate withholding, not a mistake made without awareness. Read beside the prior appeal to believe in the revelation, this gives the audience two obligations: recognize the truth and not obstruct its clear communication. It also explains why the next command is about prayer, giving and bowing together, because knowledge has to issue in practice. Mixing and concealment are not the same act. One alters what is made visible; the other withholds what ought to be visible. Together they cover speech and silence. They also prepare for the next verse, where the command moves from knowledge to prayer, giving and joining worship. Knowing what is true matters because it shapes both what is communicated and what the community does.

**Mixing truth with falsehood.**

Verse 42 explicitly shows that it is not permissible to mix truth and falsehood together in such a way that the addressee falls into a confusion as to what the truth is, and that it is forbidden to conceal the truth because of fear or greed. And do not obscure confuse the truth that I have revealed to you with falsehood that you fabricate; and do not conceal the truth the description of Muhammad wittingly that is knowing it to be the truth. Do not put truthfulness together with lying, the ap proved together with the unapproved.

**Concealing what is known.**

(nor conceal the truth while you know (the truth).) means, "Do not hide the knowledge that you have of My Messenger and what he was sent with. It is possible that it means, "...although you know the tremendous harm that this evil will cause people, misguiding them and leading them to the Fire, because they will follow the falsehood that you mixed with the truth in your claims."

**The Caliph and the reply.**

During one of his visits to the Holy town of Madīnah, the Ummayyid Caliph Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik wanted to meet someone who had lived with a Companion of the Holy Prophet if such a man was still alive. On being informed that Abu Hazim was the only man of this kind left in the town, he sent for him. "Everybody who is anybody in Madīnah has come to see me, but you haven't", complained the Caliph. "0 chief of the Muslims, may Allah protect you against saying something which is not true to the fact", replied Abu Hazim "You have not been familiar with my name before today, nor have I ever seen you. Things being what they are, how could I come to meet you? "The reason is simple," Abu Hazim said "You have made your world flourish, and turned your habitation in the other world into a desert. Said Abu Hazim, "The man who has been doing good deeds will present himself before Allah like the man who returns from a travel to his loved ones, while the man who has been doing evil deeds will appear like the slave who had run away and has now been brought back to his master." Abu Hazim replied, "Assess your deeds in the light of the Book of Allah, and you will know." "Those who are mindful of their fellow-human beings and possess the right kind of understanding to know the truth." "Fulfilling the obligations laid down by Allah, and keeping away from what He has forbidden."

**Position, the soul and the heart.**

As the Israelites were considered representatives of revealed religion in the Arab world, people used to ask them about the Arab Prophet. Pretending innocence, they would put forward such points as would turn people away from the Prophet and his mission. They used to preach to people, exhorting them to follow the truth and live their lives according to it; in practice, however, they failed to accept the truth when their turn came to do so. When a positive response to the call of God means relinquishing positions of high honour and prestige, then those who have gained religious rank through worldly elevation find it extremely difficult to follow this course. For the truly devout, however, these considerations are not a hindrance. The fulfillment that others find in worldly pleasures, true believers find in remembering God, in spending for His cause, in obeying His commandments and being steadfast in treading His path. They know full well that it is God’s punishment that is to be feared, not worldly loss. You must recognize it so as to avoid it, and you must recognize truth so as go after it. " Concerning the verse, "And confuse not truth with falsehood," the masters of the realities have said that the meaning is that you should not mix together the share of the soul and the food of the heart, for the two do not get along.

43.text:
After the warning about how known truth is handled, the passage turns to the deeds the audience is asked to perform. “Establish prayer, pay alms-tax, and bow down with those who bow down” puts regular worship, giving and joining a community in one command. “Establish prayer” is more than beginning a prayer once. It points to performing it steadily and in the proper form and time. “pay alms-tax” turns the command toward possessions, since some wealth is to be given as part of worship. The final words, “and bow down with those who bow down,” place the hearers among people already engaged in worship. The command moves from an individual act to the wider congregation without treating any one of these acts as a substitute for the others. Prayer directs the servant to God; giving makes generosity part of the same obedience; bowing with others joins personal worship to the believing community. This follows the call to believe and the warning not to mix truth with falsehood, because revelation is to shape practice, not only what people know. The next verse asks why a person may urge righteousness on others and fail to do it personally. “O Children of Israel!” identifies the community that the passage now addresses. The call names the listeners before turning to their history. “Remember ˹all˺ the favours I granted you and how I honoured you above the others” is one continuous command, so the remembered gifts and the community’s honour belong together. “Remember” asks for more than recalling dates: it asks the people to recognize the giver and let gratitude shape their conduct. “All the favours” reaches beyond a single rescue. It includes guidance through scripture and messengers, protection and victory, forgiveness, help in danger, and provision. By gathering these gifts under “all,” the verse directs the audience to consider their full history rather than selecting only the honours that flatter them. The phrase “how I honoured you above the others” then gives the special role its setting. It was connected to particular gifts and a trust: the people received God’s message and were charged with carrying His commands to others. Their honour is real, but it is not a free-standing claim that makes conduct unnecessary. The word “how” turns attention to the manner of that honour—what was given and what the people were expected to do with it. The comparison with “the others” is limited to the time and gifts in view; it is not an unrestricted ranking across every people and every age. The account can recognize a community’s past distinction without making that distinction a guarantee for every descendant. The comparison also explains why the verse joins revelation with protection and provision: the gifts were not only private comforts, but part of a public trust. Receiving guidance carried a duty toward others, so privilege and service belong to the same account. The people are asked to remember not only that they were honoured, but how that honour shaped their task. The phrase also brings visible rescue and guidance into the community’s shared memory. The blessing came first to their forefathers, yet later generations could share its effects and are addressed through that history. This link does not make the generations interchangeable: the ancestors received earlier gifts, while listeners now have to respond. The reminder begins with the community’s history, but its command is aimed at those hearing it in the present. The blessings persisted across generations, yet the decisions of each generation are its own. Remembering asks the audience to acknowledge what was received and put its guidance into practice now; gratitude is more than saying thank you, because it means responding to what was entrusted to them. That response is personal, even when the favour was communal. The verse joins memory and responsibility: the past is recalled not to secure an exemption, but to guide the present response. An inherited story can be a reason to be thankful, but it cannot supply another person’s faith or deeds. For that reason, remembering should lead to gratitude and obedience, not self-conceit or an assumption that ancestry guarantees salvation. The next verse makes the individual consequence explicit: on the Day of Judgement no soul can simply take another’s place. This warning also keeps the word “honoured” from being read as a promise that every member of a community is beyond judgement. The honour describes what was granted in history; the command to remember asks the present audience how it will respond. Gifts and accountability therefore stand together, and the line from the forefathers to their descendants carries benefits without transferring responsibility.

**The favours and their recipients.**

Verse 47 asks the Israelites to call to their minds the blessing of Allah, so that the recognition of the benefits they have received may induce them to be thankful to Allah and thus to obey Him. The verse is addressed to the Jews contemporaneous with the Holy Prophet while the blessing had been received by their forefathers. The point is that when a man receives a special favour, his children and grand children too usually partake of the benefits flowing from it; in this sense, the Jews who are being addressed may be said to have received the blessing themselves. This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God’s chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world. 48.text:
“Guard yourselves against the Day on which no soul will be of help to another” begins with a command for the present and names the Day of Judgement as its reason. To guard against it means responding while action is still possible, not expecting someone else to rescue us after the final account begins. “No intercession will be accepted, no ransom taken, and no help will be given” then names three forms of help a person might expect: an appeal by another, a payment, or the support of a powerful friend. No soul can settle another person’s account or take its place. Intercession is not denied in every case, but it cannot be demanded or guaranteed; it is accepted only by God’s permission. The word “accepted” matters: the verse does not set up a negotiation between equal parties. A person cannot compel intercession or treat it as an entitlement; any such aid remains subject to God’s permission. Nor can kinship or inherited status turn an appeal into a right. Nor can prayers or fasts be transferred from one person to make up another’s obligations. “No ransom taken” excludes wealth as a way to buy release: even a vast payment cannot undo a person’s record. “No help will be given” completes the list, closing off the hope that some other ally can override the judgement. These are not claims that friends never help in ordinary life. The contrast is between assistance that can matter in this world and the final account where no one controls another person’s outcome. The warning follows the reminder of the favours in the preceding verse. Those gifts do not turn into a family guarantee; each person remains responsible for faith and conduct. The order of the clauses matters: first the verse names the Day, then it rules out another’s intervention, payment, and any remaining help. That sequence makes clear what “Guard yourselves” asks of the listeners now: follow God’s directions and avoid what He has prohibited. The point is not to despair of every aid; intercession remains under God’s permission. The point is to refuse the assumption that wealth, status, kinship, or a powerful friend can substitute for one’s own response before judgement. The words “no soul will be of help to another” and “no intercession will be accepted” must be read together: no person controls the outcome, even though intercession can occur only with God’s permission. The warning is therefore not a denial of every possible aid, but a call to prepare before the Day arrives, when no person can take another’s place. The image of the earth filled with gold makes the point concrete: even immeasurable wealth cannot purchase release. In this way, the verse brings the memory of earlier favour into an urgent personal question: what is each listener doing with the guidance already received?

**The Day of Judgement.**

After Allah reminded the Children of Israel of the favors that He has granted them, He warned them about the duration of the torment which He will punish them with on the Day of Resurrection. Verse 47 asks the Israelites to call to their minds the blessing of Allah, so that the recognition of the benefits they have received may induce them to be thankful to Allah and thus to obey Him. The day referred to in verse 48 is the Day of Judgment. As for no one being able to suffice another on that day, the phrase should be understood in the sense of one man paying the dues on behalf of another man. Let us, for example, suppose that a man is found wanting in the performance of obligatory acts of worship like Salah and Sawm (fasting), and another man should suggest that his own prayers and fasts may be transferred to the account of the former in order to make up the deficiency. Such a transaction shall not be possible on that day. Protect yourselves against the Day of Judgement by following Allah’s instructions and staying away from what He has prohibited. On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. (O mankind! Have Taqwa of your Lord (by keeping your duty to Him and avoiding all evil), and fear a Day when no father can avail aught for his son, nor a son avail aught for his father)(31:33). He will then award the evil deed its kind and will multiply the good deeds. It will not be accepted of them, even if they paid the earth's fill of gold as ransom. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. To think that anything other than good deeds will avail one, is to underestimate the rigours of that Day.

49.text:
“˹Remember˺ how We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with dreadful torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women” begins the recollection with the suffering that made rescue necessary. The first word, “Remember,” brings an event from the forefathers’ past into the present duties of their descendants. “We delivered you” is addressed to later generations through what their ancestors endured: they can share the benefit of the rescue, but their inheritance does not replace their own response. “The people of Pharaoh” identifies the power responsible for the oppression. The account is not simply about an escape from Egypt; it is about a ruler and his people using their authority to humiliate and harm an entire community. “Dreadful torment” is then made concrete. “Slaughtering your sons” points to the killing of newborn boys, while “keeping your women” does not describe a kindness: the women were left alive for service, and the policy was driven by Pharaoh’s self-interest. The killing is connected to Pharaoh’s fear that a child born among the Israelites would end his rule. One account also recalls a dream that Pharaoh understood as a warning, followed by orders to kill the boys and assign the people degrading work. The final words, “That was a severe test from your Lord,” can refer to the calamity of the slaughter or to the blessing of being delivered from Pharaoh. In the first reading, patience is tested by suffering; in the second, gratitude is tested by rescue. Those are not morally equivalent events: the verse names oppression as cruelty and deliverance as favour. Calling both a test keeps the whole history together without confusing the harm with the mercy that ended it. The phrase “from your Lord” also directs attention to the one who brought the rescue, rather than treating survival as a reason for pride. The account now moves from the violence of Pharaoh’s rule to the means of escape: the next verse describes the sea being parted and the pursuers drowned. The present audience is therefore asked to remember both the suffering its forefathers faced and the deliverance that followed, and to respond to that history with patience in hardship and gratitude for favour. The repeated command to remember does not erase the past or turn oppression into a gift; it makes the rescue and the people’s responsibility visible together. The two verbs “slaughtering” and “keeping” place distinct harms side by side: one group was marked for death, while the other was held under the ruler’s control. The women’s survival did not mean freedom; it was part of the way Pharaoh used the community. This makes the word “delivered” larger than a simple move from place to place: the people had to be freed from the threat of death as well as the humiliation of forced work. The order of phrases traces the harm from Pharaoh’s rule to its effect on families, and only then asks how the whole episode was a test. The next verse completes the sequence by showing the pursuers destroyed, so the history moves from oppression to escape and then to safety. Remembering this return from danger is part of the favour being recalled. The two readings also explain why “dreadful torment” comes before “severe test”: first the human harm is named plainly, and only then is the response or rescue discussed. The language does not present the victims’ suffering as a benefit; it presents deliverance as mercy within a painful history. For descendants who did not witness the event, remembering is a way to inherit responsibility, not a claim to automatic reward.

**The favour shown to the forefathers.**

Verse 47 had spoken of the special favours shown to the Israelites by Allah. Now, with Verse 49 begins the account of these favours. (Remember My favor which I bestowed upon you). So Allah mentioned saving their children from being slaughtered in order to remind them of the many favors that He granted them. He selected them for a special task: they were to receive God’s scriptures and pass His commandments on to the rest of mankind. In relation to this office, they were granted many other blessings and facilities: victory over their enemies, forgiveness of their sins, special help in times of peril, divine provision for their physical needs, and so on. This misled later generations of Jews into thinking that they were God’s chosen people, and were assured of salvation in the next world. But such matters as salvation are not a hereditary right of any group. Successive generations are to be judged on their own merits. On the Day of Judgement people will be judged individually, according to their actions. To think that anything other than good deeds will avail one, is to underestimate the rigours of that Day.

**Pharaoh's torment.**

After the dream, Pharaoh ordered that every newborn male among the Children of Israel be killed and that the girls be left alone. He also commanded that the Children of Israel be given tasks of hard labor and assigned the most humiliating jobs. It was also said that it means, "They used to exaggerate in tormenting you" according to Al-Qurtubi. We should state here that 'Pharaoh' (Fir'awn) is a title that was given to every disbelieving king who ruled Egypt, whether from the 'Amaliq (Canaanites) or otherwise, just as Caesar (Qaysar) is the title of the disbelieving kings who ruled Rome and Damascus. Someone had made a prediction to the Pharaoh that a child was going to be born among the Israelites who would destroy his kingship. So, he began slaughtering all the male infants as soon as they were born. But he would spare the females, as there was nothing to fear from them, and, moreover, they could, on growing up, serve as maid-servants. So, even this leniency was motivated by self-interest. Remember when Allah saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who were tormenting you, slaughtering your sons so you would not survive, and letting your women live so they could serve them, taking great pains to humiliate and insult you.

**Calamity and blessing as a test.**

What the verse refers to as "a great trial" is either the slaughter of the sons - which was a calamity, and it is the quality of patience that is tested in a calamity - or the deliverance from the people of the Pharaoh - which was a blessing, and it is the quality of thankfulness which is tested when one receives a blessing. (That was a tremendous trial from your Lord), a tremendous calamity from your Lord; and it is also said this means: a tremendous blessing. When you were saved from the oppression of Pharaoh and his people, it was a great test for you from your Lord, to see if you would be thankful. And for you therein was a tremendous trial from your Lord: It is said that [it was] a great blessing niʿmatun ʿaẓīma and a severe trial miḥnatun shadīda. In truth what [came] from God was externally a trial miḥna but it was really for the one who recognized it a blessing niʿma and a kindness minna. (And We tried them with good (blessings) and evil (calamities) in order that they might turn (to obey Allah.)(7:168). The children of Israel were patient in enduring injury from Pharaoh and his people so He appointed prophets from among them and made them kings. He gave them what He had not given anyone in all the worlds. The next verse gives us the details about this deliverance.

“And ˹remember˺ when We parted the sea, rescued you” connects this event to the preceding account: deliverance from Pharaoh’s oppression did not end when the Israelites left Egypt. The people were pursued, and the sea stood between them and safety. “We parted the sea” names the way forward; “rescued you” states what that opening made possible. The verse then turns to the pursuers: “and drowned Pharaoh’s people before your very eyes” describes the fate of the army that followed into the sea and emphasizes that the people saw the outcome themselves. The whole movement matters: the way opened for them, they crossed, and the danger behind them was removed. The same event was escape for one people and ruin for the army that pursued them. The scene is not only an account of geography or military defeat. The phrase “rescued you” places the people at the center of what the opening made possible, while the ending asks them to recognize the fate of the pursuers. The story invites remembrance of both the saved and the lost. Remembering the parting alone would leave the threat unfinished; remembering only the drowning would hide why the path opened. Both outcomes are part of one deliverance, bringing relief to the Israelites and humiliation to their enemy. It also links the two verses: the rescue named after Pharaoh’s torment is now shown in detail, from the moment the sea divided to the end of the pursuit. The people are asked to remember not simply a narrow passage through water, but the complete reversal of their danger. This explains why the enemy’s fate appears beside the people’s escape rather than the verse ending when the sea opens. The rescue is complete only when the army can no longer pursue them. “Remember” points to the result as well as the route: the people are to recall who made a way and how the threat ended. A later observance carries this rescue into new generations through worship, gratitude, and shared remembrance beyond the eyewitnesses of the event.

**The sea and the escape.**

He, in his capacity as a messenger of Allah, continued efforts for a long time to make the Pharaoh and his people see Truth, but when they persisted in their denial, Allah commanded him to take the Israelites along with him and leave Egypt surreptitiously. On their way, they came across a sea while the Pharaoh was behind him with his army in hot pursuit. Allah commanded the sea to split, and make way for Sayyidna Musa and his people. And remember when We divided split in two for you on account of you the sea such that you were able to cross it and escape from your enemy; and We delivered you from drowning and drowned Pharaoh’s folk his people with him while you were beholding the sea crashing down on top of them. Remember Allah’s favour in saving you when He parted the sea and made it a dry path for you to go through, while drowning your enemies, Pharaoh and his followers, before your very eyes, as you looked on. When We divided for you the sea and We delivered you and drowned Pharaoh's folk while you were beholding.

**The pursuit and drowning.**

But when the Pharaoh and his army followed them into the sea, it gathered the water back so that the Pharaoh and his men were drowned then and there. (And (remember) when We separated the sea for you and saved you and drowned Fir'awn's (Pharaoh) people while you were watching) means, 'After We saved you from Fir'awn and you escaped with Musa; Fir'awn went out in your pursuit and We parted the sea for you.' Allah mentioned this story in detail, as we will come to know, Allah willing. (And saved you) meaning, "We saved you from them, drowning them while you watched, bringing relief to your hearts and humiliation to your enemy." What a difference [there is] between one who sees with his own eyes yet doubts and one who only hears [about something] and yet sees it like an eyewitness because of the power of his belief!

**The rescue remembered.**

It was reported that the day the Children of Israel were saved from Fir'awn was called the day of 'Ashura'. Imam Ahmad reported that Ibn 'Abbas said that the Messenger of Allah came to Al-Madīnah and found that the Jews were fasting the day of 'Ashura'. So the Messenger of Allah fasted that day and ordered that it be fasted.
